label: Geodesics and Geodesic Curvature
notes: Open by posing the chapter's single question on printed pages 115 to 129: of all the bending a surface curve exhibits, how much is forced by the surface and how much is the curve veering inside it. Preview the normal-plus-geodesic split as the answer.

label: A Curve on a Surface
notes: Make the Darboux frame tangible before any measurement. Walk the class through the unit tangent along the path, the surface normal pointing off the surface, and the in-surface side vector completing the orthonormal triple. Stress that every later decomposition resolves acceleration against exactly these three axes.

label: Splitting the Curvature Vector
notes: Show that an arc-length curve's acceleration is its curvature vector with no tangential part. Project it onto the normal for normal curvature and onto the side vector for geodesic curvature, then derive the Pythagorean identity, emphasising why the cross term vanishes by orthogonality.

label: Normal Curvature and Meusnier
notes: Explain that normal curvature is fixed by tangent direction alone because it comes from the second fundamental form. Present Meusnier's theorem with the tilted-circle picture: curves sharing a tangent have centers on a circle, the normal section being the largest osculating circle.

label: Geodesic Curvature as Sideways Turning
notes: Define geodesic curvature as the intrinsic side-turning rate of the tangent, ignoring the forced bending into space. Emphasise its invariance under isometric flexing, so a surface inhabitant could measure it with rulers alone. This intrinsic nature is what makes it the right straightness measure.

label: Geodesics: The Straightest Curves
notes: State the definition: geodesic curvature identically zero, so acceleration is purely normal. Use the sphere to contrast a great circle, which is geodesic, with a latitude circle, which curves sideways. Warn that geodesics are locally straightest but not always globally shortest paths.

label: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Measurement
notes: Present two observers computing geodesic curvature: an external one resolving the space acceleration along the side vector, and an internal one using only the metric. Argue they must agree, because the metric already encodes the side-turning rate, making this a small but important theorem.

label: The Sticky-Tape Construction
notes: Use the tactile tape model: a strip pressed flat along the curve lies without wrinkling precisely along a geodesic. Then develop, or unroll, the surface onto a plane so geodesics become literal straight lines. This is the most physical test for vanishing geodesic curvature.

label: Surfaces of Revolution
notes: Specialise to surfaces of revolution generated by spinning a profile curve. Introduce meridians and parallels as natural coordinates, the radius from the axis, and the angle the geodesic makes with meridians. Note meridians are geodesics by symmetry while parallels usually are not.

label: Clairaut's Relation
notes: Derive Clairaut's relation that radius times sine of the meridian angle stays constant along any geodesic. Frame it as a conservation law from rotational symmetry, the surface analogue of angular momentum, and read off the barrier radius where the geodesic reaches ninety degrees and turns back.

label: Kepler, Angular Momentum, and Clairaut
notes: Draw the analogy between Clairaut's invariant and Kepler's second law. Rotational symmetry of the surface plays the role of the central force, so swept-rate constancy becomes constant radius times sine of the angle. Use it to predict barrier radii and the bouncing of bound geodesics.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Recap the three pillars: the curvature split into normal and geodesic parts, geodesics as the zero-geodesic-curvature curves verified by tape and unrolling, and Clairaut's invariant governing surfaces of revolution. Close by previewing how geodesic curvature feeds the upcoming Gauss-Bonnet accounting of total curvature.
